Colossians
kuh-LOSH-unz
noun (proper)
From Greek Kolossaeis (Κολοσσαεῖς), the inhabitants of Colossae — a city in the Lycus Valley of the Roman province of Asia, southeast of Laodicea; the name of Paul's canonical letter to the church planted there by Epaphras (Col 1:7), the most concentrated Christological epistle in the Pauline corpus.

See also: Colossians

Biblical Definition

The Epistle to the Colossians is one of Paul's four prison letters, written from Rome circa AD 60–62 alongside Ephesians, Philippians, and Philemon. The church at Colossae had not been founded by Paul directly but by Epaphras, and was threatened by a syncretistic error — a “Colossian heresy” blending Jewish ceremonialism, speculative angelology, ascetic ordinances, and mystical visionary experience. Paul answers with the most concentrated Christological statement in all his letters: “Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature: for in Him all things were created” (Col 1:15–16). Christ is not one rung on a heavenly ladder but the singular source, sustainer, and goal of all creation. The body of the letter applies this cosmic Christology downward to the local and domestic: false dietary and calendar regulations are dismissed as shadows (Col 2:16–17); household relations are ordered on the principle of Christ's lordship (wives, husbands, children, servants); and the church is commanded to let the word of Christ dwell richly, teaching and admonishing one another (Col 3:16). The letter's anti-speculative, Christ-sufficient posture is the Reformed confessional church's standing rebuke of every theological novelty that supplements Christ with additional mediators, esoteric attainments, or ascetic merit. “For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily.” (Col 2:9) — this single verse is the death of all Gnostic intermediary systems and their modern heirs.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster does not record “Colossians” as a common English word; it is a proper noun — the inhabitants of Colossae and the title of Paul's canonical epistle to that church, distinguished by its exalted Christology and its refutation of early syncretic error.

expand to see more

COLOSSIANS, n. pl. [From Colossae, a city of ancient Phrygia.] The inhabitants of Colossae; specifically, the recipients of Paul's canonical letter — one of the four prison epistles of the New Testament, notable for its anti-speculative Christology against a proto-Gnostic blend of Jewish ceremonialism, angel worship, and ascetic mysticism.

The letter stands as the New Testament's most sustained argument that the fullness of God — every divine perfection — dwells bodily and exclusively in Christ, leaving no room for supplementary spiritual hierarchies or ascetic ladders of attainment.

Puritan and Reformed commentators (John Owen, Thomas Goodwin, John Lightfoot) read Colossians' anti-speculative principle as the standing rule for every age: whatever claims to add spiritual attainment, hidden knowledge, or visionary experience beyond the word of Christ is “not holding fast to the Head” (Col 2:19).

Key Scripture

Col 1:15 — "Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature:"

Col 1:17 — "And he is before all things, and by him all things consist."

Col 2:8 — "Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ."

Col 2:9 — "For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily."

Modern Corruption

The Colossian heresy has modern heirs: New Apostolic Reformation mysticism, Word-Faith attainment theology, and progressive projects that add political or therapeutic criteria to the sufficiency of Christ all mirror the ancient error.

expand to see more

The Colossian error — supplementing Christ with angelic mediators, dietary law, and private visionary access — has diversified rather than died. Modern parallels include charismatic “throne room” mysticism claiming ongoing prophetic access beyond Scripture, New Apostolic Reformation teaching that adds contemporary apostles and prophets as required mediators, Roman Catholic Mariology and the invocation of saints as intercessors, and prosperity-gospel teaching that demands positive confession as a mechanism for divine provision. Each in its own register adds something to the all-sufficient Christ that Paul refused to permit in Colossae.

Progressive evangelicalism adds a socio-political dimension: the fullness of Christ's lordship is redefined as requiring ideological commitments — antiracist frameworks, social-justice activism — as indices of genuine Christian faith. Colossians answers: the fullness dwells bodily in Christ, not in political supplementation. Reformed orthodoxy applies Paul's anti-speculative principle to every age: Christ alone is sufficient; the word of Christ dwelling richly in the assembly is the church's full treasure (Col 3:16).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Rooted in the name of the ancient Phrygian city Colossae and the Greek eikon (“image”) and plērōma (“fullness”) — the epistle's two controlling Christological terms.

expand to see more

Colossae — a city in the Lycus Valley of ancient Phrygia, modern southwest Turkey; home to a Pauline congregation founded by Epaphras, eclipsed by neighboring Laodicea but significant in Pauline correspondence

Greek eikon (εἰκών) — image, visible representation; applied to Christ in Col 1:15 as the perfect image of the invisible God, the living display of the divine nature in human form

Greek plērōma (πλήρωμα) — fullness, totality; the anti-Gnostic term Paul claims for Christ alone in Col 2:9 — all divine fullness resides bodily in Him, not distributed across a hierarchy of powers

Greek prōtotokos (πρωτότοκος) — firstborn; denotes supremacy and priority over all creation, not temporal derivation from the Father — the title of sovereign preeminence

Paul's imprisonment — the four prison epistles (Colossians, Ephesians, Philippians, Philemon) were written from Roman captivity, giving their pastoral gravity the weight of a martyr's testimony

Usage

"Colossians' Christological hymn (1:15–20) is the New Testament's answer to every system that places Christ at the top of a hierarchy rather than as the singular Lord over all hierarchies — He is before all things and in Him all things hold together."

"The letter's warning against “philosophy and vain deceit” (Col 2:8) is the standing biblical criterion by which Reformed theology tests every doctrinal novelty: does it add to or subtract from the all-sufficient Christ whose word is to dwell richly in the assembly?"

"The household code in Colossians 3:18–4:1 anchors every domestic order — including wifely submission and paternal authority — in the phrase “as is fitting in the Lord,” grounding created order in the living lordship of the risen Christ."
